explanations.explanation: The ram's horn it is! The watchman sees the sword coming and blows it to warn the people (Ezekiel 33:3). No charger, no Wi-Fi, no group text. Just a horn and a good set of lungs.

A signal fire is a smart idea, and I know fire, I work with ovens all day. But that's not what the text says. The watchman sees the sword coming and blows the ram's horn to warn the people (Ezekiel 33:3).

explanations.answer: He runs from house to house
explanations.explanation: Knocking on every door sounds like a very long day, friend. The text has something quicker: the watchman blows the ram's horn to warn the people (Ezekiel 33:3). One blast, and he doesn't have to wear out his sandals.

His own head. The man heard the horn, ignored the warning, and God says “his blood will be on his own head.” (Ezekiel 33:4). The warning was given and he had his chance. I think this is a heavy line, so I'll leave it plain.
Not the neighbor. God says the man's blood will be on his own head (Ezekiel 33:4). He heard the horn himself, and that's why it lands on him. It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it plain.

The king doesn't show up in this verse at all. God says the blood will be on the man's own head (Ezekiel 33:4). He's the one who heard the horn and ignored the warning. It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it plain.

Life. God says that if the man had heeded the warning, “he would have saved his life.” (Ezekiel 33:5). Listening to that horn was all that stood between him and the sword. It's a serious line, so I'll just let it sit there.
Home is an easy one to guess, since nobody wants to lose their house. But verse 5 says the man would have saved his life (Ezekiel 33:5). What's at stake here is bigger than any roof.
Land makes sense as a guess, because verse 2 talks about a whole land. But verse 5 says the man would have saved his life (Ezekiel 33:5). It's his life on the line, not his property.

The watchman. He saw the sword coming and never blew the horn, so God says, “I will hold the watchman accountable for his blood.” (Ezekiel 33:6). The person who is taken away is taken “in his iniquity,” and the watchman is still held accountable. That's the whole job, friend: see it, sound it.

The people are the ones the watchman was supposed to warn. In this what-if, God says the one who is taken away goes in his iniquity, but He will hold the watchman accountable for his blood (Ezekiel 33:6). The horn never sounded, so the watchman is the one in the hot seat.

No king in this verse. God says He will hold the watchman accountable for the blood of the one the sword takes (Ezekiel 33:6). The person who saw the sword coming and stayed quiet is the one God names.

The house of Israel. God tells Ezekiel, the man He is speaking to, “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 33:7). I bet that was a surprise! He came for a what-if and walked out with a job title.
Babylon isn't named in this verse. God says He has made Ezekiel a watchman “for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 33:7). Those are the people he's watching over.
Egypt doesn't come up here. God says He has made Ezekiel a watchman “for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 33:7). That's who the warning is for.

True. God tells Ezekiel to “hear the word from My mouth and give them the warning from Me.” (Ezekiel 33:7). Ezekiel isn't making this up as he goes. He's the delivery guy, and the package comes from God.

This one is actually true. God tells Ezekiel, “so hear the word from My mouth and give them the warning from Me.” (Ezekiel 33:7). The warning comes from God Himself. Ezekiel's job is to pass it along.

explanations.answer: God will hold him accountable for the man's blood
explanations.explanation: That's right. If God says a wicked man will surely die and Ezekiel doesn't speak up, the man dies in his iniquity, “yet I will hold you accountable for his blood.” (Ezekiel 33:8). That's a lot to carry. I get nervous when somebody hands me their coat to hold.

explanations.answer: God will choose a new watchman in his place
explanations.explanation: God doesn't mention a replacement. He says the wicked man will die in his iniquity, “yet I will hold you accountable for his blood.” (Ezekiel 33:8). The watchman has the job, and it's on him.

explanations.answer: God will overlook it this one time
explanations.explanation: Verse 8 doesn't say that. It says the wicked man dies in his iniquity, “yet I will hold you accountable for his blood.” (Ezekiel 33:8). The text gives no one-time pass.

Close, but it goes the other way. If Ezekiel warns the wicked man and he doesn't turn, “he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your life.” (Ezekiel 33:9). Ezekiel did the warning, so he's clear. The choice to turn belongs to the man.

False, and I'm glad. God says if Ezekiel warns the wicked man and he doesn't turn, “he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your life.” (Ezekiel 33:9). Ezekiel's part is the warning. After that, the man has to decide what to do with it.

Their transgressions and their sins. They say, “Our transgressions and our sins are heavy upon us, and we are wasting away because of them!” (Ezekiel 33:10). That's honest. They know exactly what's weighing on them.

explanations.answer: The long years far from home
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd guess that, but it's not what they say. In verse 10 they say, “Our transgressions and our sins are heavy upon us” (Ezekiel 33:10). What's weighing on them is their sins.
Foreign kings aren't what they bring up. The people say, “Our transgressions and our sins are heavy upon us” (Ezekiel 33:10). It's their own sins they're pointing at.
The death of the wicked. God says, “As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11). Read that one slowly, friend. I did, twice.
Verse 11 doesn't mention prayers or the proud. What God says is, “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11). That's the answer to the people's question.
Offerings and the careless don't come up in this verse. God says, “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11). That's what He tells them.

Turn goes in the first blank. God says He wants “…that the wicked should turn from their ways and live.” (Ezekiel 33:11). It's the word He keeps coming back to in this verse. Turning is what He's asking for.
Live goes in the second blank. God says He wants “…that the wicked should turn from their ways and live.” (Ezekiel 33:11). That's His answer to a people asking, “How can we live?” (Ezekiel 33:10).
Learning is a fine thing, but it's not the word in verse 11. God says He wants “…that the wicked should turn from their ways and live.” (Ezekiel 33:11). The word He uses is turn.
Waiting is great for cookie dough, but it isn't what God says here. He wants “…that the wicked should turn from their ways and live.” (Ezekiel 33:11). The word is turn, not wait.
Rest sounds lovely after a long day at the bakery. But God doesn't say it here. He wants “…that the wicked should turn from their ways and live.” (Ezekiel 33:11).

Not quite, friend. God says “The righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in the day of his transgression” (Ezekiel 33:12). Yesterday's perfect batch doesn't unburn today's tray. His past righteousness won't deliver him on that day.

False, and you read it right. God says “The righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in the day of his transgression” (Ezekiel 33:12). He adds that the righteous man won't “be able to survive by his righteousness on the day he sins.” Past righteousness doesn't deliver him.

True. God says “neither will the wickedness of the wicked man cause him to stumble on the day he turns from his wickedness” (Ezekiel 33:12). The day he turns, the old wickedness won't trip him up. That's a fresh start in plain words.

This one is true, friend. God says “neither will the wickedness of the wicked man cause him to stumble on the day he turns from his wickedness” (Ezekiel 33:12). When a wicked man turns, his old wickedness won't make him stumble that day.

explanations.answer: None of them will be remembered
explanations.explanation: None of them. God says, “none of his righteous works will be remembered; he will die because of the iniquity he has committed.” (Ezekiel 33:13). That's what happens when the righteous man trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity. It's a sobering verse.

That's not what the verse says. God says, “none of his righteous works will be remembered; he will die because of the iniquity he has committed.” (Ezekiel 33:13). His righteous works don't cover anything.

Verse 13 says nothing about a lighter sentence. God says, “none of his righteous works will be remembered; he will die because of the iniquity he has committed.” (Ezekiel 33:13). His works aren't remembered.

explanations.answer: He pays back what he stole
explanations.explanation: He pays it back. God says the man who turns “makes restitution for what he has stolen” (Ezekiel 33:15). He also restores a pledge and walks in the statutes of life without practicing iniquity. That's turning with receipts.

No bulls in this list. In verse 15 the man restores a pledge, makes restitution for what he has stolen, and walks in the statutes of life without practicing iniquity (Ezekiel 33:15). That's what turning looks like here.

Fasting isn't mentioned in these verses. God says the man restores a pledge, makes restitution for what he has stolen, and walks in the statutes of life without practicing iniquity (Ezekiel 33:15). That's the turning.
It is not just. That's what they say: “The way of the Lord is not just.” (Ezekiel 33:17). After everything God just laid out, that's quite the plot twist, friend. They said it anyway.
Slow isn't their complaint. Verse 17 says, “Yet your people say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’” (Ezekiel 33:17). That's what they say.
Strict isn't the word they use. They say, “The way of the Lord is not just.” (Ezekiel 33:17). That's their charge.
Not quite. God doesn't agree with them. He says, “But it is their way that is not just.” (Ezekiel 33:17). The people said His way is not just, and God says their way is the one that isn't.
False. God doesn't agree with them at all. He says, “But it is their way that is not just.” (Ezekiel 33:17). He puts the word just on their way, not His.
Ways. God says, “But I will judge each of you according to his ways, O house of Israel.” (Ezekiel 33:20). He says each of you, one by one. It's about how each person walks.
Tribe isn't in this verse. God says, “But I will judge each of you according to his ways, O house of Israel.” (Ezekiel 33:20). He judges each person by his ways.
Family isn't the word here. God says, “But I will judge each of you according to his ways, O house of Israel.” (Ezekiel 33:20). It comes down to each person's own ways.
